brief: The piece argues the 2026 midterm results reflect affordability and accountability concerns rather than a durable realignment: youth-male and Hispanic-women swings away from the 2024 coalition, and persistent unfavorable views of Democrats, show support must be continually earned. It then applies the same consent-based logic to AI buildout politics. Midterm losses and state-level permitting fights (Texas's moratorium threat versus Pennsylvania's faster track for projects meeting affordability/community standards) raise the odds of delay; the author's base case is longer delays, tougher conditions and selective resumption, with some projects relocated or abandoned. Therefore, restricting incremental capacity should support the scarcity value of compute already operating, shifting preference toward hyperscalers with secure power and monetisation routes over capacity still awaiting permitting and financing (hyperscalers outperformed semis this week). Slower delivery leaves component production ahead of installation, exposing hardware suppliers to deferrals and excess inventory even as usable compute stays scarce. The author stays constructive on long-term AI demand but increasingly selective on where the resulting economic rents accrue.
